props.title: Shall We Dance
props.initialSlug: Fred & Ginger dazzle in shipboard romance romp

sections.content: Shall We Dance represents the pinnacle of Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers' collaborative magic at RKO Pictures. Their seventh pairing showcases George Gershwin's final film score before his untimely death, featuring standout numbers like "They Can't Take That Away from Me" and "Let's Call the Whole Thing Off." The plot - involving an American ballet dancer posing as a Russian and falling for a tap dancer - might be thin, but director Mark Sandrich crafts ingenious scenarios for the dance sequences, including the iconic roller-skating routine and the engine room tap number that transforms industrial machinery into percussion.

sections.content: The film marks a crucial evolution in the Hollywood musical, bridging the gap between earlier backstage narratives and integrated storytelling where songs advance the plot. Follow the Fleet (1936) and The Story of Vernon and Irene Castle (1939) bookend this period, but Shall We Dance achieves the most sophisticated blend of romance, comedy and pure dance spectacle. The Gershwin score elevates every moment, while the art deco sets by Van Nest Polglase create a glamorous playground for the leads' physicality. SUBHEAD: Innovation in Dance Film Technique

Sandrich's camera movement and editing techniques in Shall We Dance influenced decades of dance films that followed. The way he captures full-body movement while maintaining intimate facial expressions became a template, visible in everything from Cover Girl (1944) to The Band Wagon (1953). The film's innovative use of multiple cameras to catch every nuance of the dance numbers, particularly in "They All Laughed," set new standards for filming musical performance. This technical sophistication paired perfectly with Astaire's famous insistence on shooting dance numbers in as few takes as possible, maintaining the flow and energy of live performance.
